 Government to Centralize LPG Subsidy for Genuine Consumers
 Ratopati
 November 07, 2026
 Read in Nepali
 Kathmandu. The billions of rupees in subsidy that the state has been providing on cooking (LPG) gas to make the kitchens of ordinary citizens easier will now be focused on actual consumers.
 Concluding that for years, the facility provided from the state treasury in the name of the poor and common citizens has been benefiting star hotels, large restaurants, and industrial establishments, the government and Nepal Oil Corporation are preparing to take a strong step of policy reform.
 Now, the gas subsidy provided to profitable commercial sectors will be completely abolished, and the amount saved will be used to secure the kitchens of ordinary citizens, stabilize gas prices, and provide further concessions to the target group. For this, the corporation has brought the homework of implementing a dual pricing system in the market and separate cylinders for domestic and commercial use to the final stage.
 Businesses are getting double benefits, Corporation facing billions in loss 
 Currently, Nepal Oil Corporation sells one cylinder of 14.2 kg capacity LPG gas to both ordinary consumers and commercial establishments at the same price of Rs 2,060. However, when the international market purchase rate, transportation, and other taxes and administrative expenses are added, the actual cost (landed cost) of one cylinder of gas for the corporation is around Rs 2,700. This means the corporation is selling gas at a loss of approximately Rs 640 per cylinder.
 Ordinary citizens do not receive any financial benefit by paying Rs 2,060 to use gas. However, commercial establishments doing business worth billions not only get gas at the same subsidized price but also get Value Added Tax (VAT) refunded from the state by showing the amount spent on gas purchase as 'business expense'.
 Binita Mani Upadhyay, Director of Nepal Oil Corporation, clarified that this double benefit being received by the commercial sector will now stop. 'Consumers pay the same price as ordinary citizens, large hotels and industries also buy gas at the same subsidized price. Moreover, they also get the benefit of VAT refund,' said Director Upadhyay. 'This means that profitable businesses are getting more benefits than ordinary citizens, which is a direct misuse of the subsidy. Now, gas consumed in the commercial sector will be sold at the landed cost (cost price), which will reduce the corporation's loss and make it easier to provide concessions to ordinary citizens.'
 New policy to make ordinary citizens' kitchens cheaper 
 According to the corporation's data, a large portion of the total LPG gas imported into the country is consumed in the commercial sector. If the gas used for commercial and industrial purposes is sold at full cost price, billions of rupees of the state will be saved.
 This saved amount will not only reduce the corporation's accumulated losses but will also act as a 'Price Stabilization Fund' to prevent price increases in Nepali kitchens even when gas prices rise in the international market. This ensures that ordinary consumers will directly benefit from the cessation of commercial discounts. Under this plan, the government recently proposed to the gas industrialists, in discussions, to distribute 30 percent of the total gas trade through commercial cylinders at the landed cost.
 Industrialists' Counter Proposal: Test with 10 Percent 
 Regarding the government's proposal to make 30 percent commercial cylinders, the Nepal LP Gas Industry Association has submitted a counter-proposal, citing some practical difficulties. The association has formally sent a letter to the Executive Director of Nepal Oil Corporation suggesting testing this policy starting with 10 percent instead of immediately reaching 30 percent.
 In the letter signed by Amit Agarwal, the association's general secretary, the option of selling gas at the landed cost to everyone and providing direct cash subsidy to the actual consumers through the banking system has also been emphasized. 'It would be scientific to provide direct cash to the target group through commercial banks by selling gas at the landed cost,' stated General Secretary Agarwal in the letter. 'Even if it is through cylinders, let's start by allocating 10 percent of the total quota for commercial use and the remaining 90 percent for domestic use for now. The percentage of commercial gas can be adjusted in the future based on market conditions.'
 Technical Debate on Cylinder Color and Size 
 The main technical question is how to differentiate domestic and commercial cylinders when implementing dual pricing. Currently, there are about 1.5 to 2 crore cylinders of 14.2 kg capacity in the market. The government wants to bring separate cylinders of larger capacity (19 kg, 50 kg, or 450 kg) into use for commercial purposes.
 However, Dewan Bahadur Chand, president of the Gas Industry Association, says that introducing new cylinders overnight will cause chaos in the market. 'We are not against the government's plan, but if separate sized cylinders are introduced for hotels and commercial purposes, the smaller cylinders will be displaced, increasing the number and complicating management,' says President Chand. 'Therefore, we can paint the existing 14.2 kg cylinders red for domestic use and blue for commercial use. The industrialists are ready to bear the cost of painting.'
 The association has also demanded at least two years' time for the industry to prepare if the government insists on using cylinders of different weights. On the other hand, corporation officials point out the risk that commercial establishments might hide and use subsidized red cylinders even if blue-colored cylinders are used initially. Therefore, the corporation's stance is that commercial sectors must be mandated to use larger cylinders in the long run.
 The concept of red and blue cylinders for gas is not new in Nepal. Similar dual pricing and cash subsidy policies were proposed during the governments led by Khilraj Regmi and Dr. Baburam Bhattarai. However, due to the lack of accurate household data and a very weak monitoring mechanism, those policies failed completely.
